# Sergey Turlo

<div class="position">
Postdoctoral Researcher in Quantitative Marketing
</div>

<div class="institution">
Goethe University Frankfurt
</div>

I study how consumers acquire and process information and how firms design information environments. My research focuses on information frictions and their implications for consumer choice, firm strategy, and market outcomes.

Methodologically, I combine rational inattention and discrete-choice models with Bayesian methods, experiments, and economic theory.



 

:::


## Job Market Paper

::: {.paper}

### Demand Estimation with Costly Attribute Information Integration

<div class="paper-meta">
with Matteo Fina, Arash Laghaie, Johannes Kasinger, and Thomas Otter
</div>

We develop a discrete-choice framework in which consumers optimally decide how much product information to process before choosing. Using a controlled choice experiment, we show how accounting for endogenous information processing changes demand estimation and helps explain choice patterns that are difficult to reconcile with standard random-utility models.

[Paper →](files/turlo-demand-estimation.pdf){.paper-link}

:::


## Selected Research

::: {.paper}

### Discrete Choice in Marketing through the Lens of Rational Inattention

<div class="paper-meta">
with Matteo Fina, Johannes Kasinger, Arash Laghaie, and Thomas Otter<br>
<em>Quantitative Marketing and Economics</em>, 23(1), 45–104, 2025
</div>

We develop an empirical rational-inattention framework for discrete-choice data in which consumers optimally allocate attention across alternatives and product attributes. The framework provides a tractable way to incorporate costly information processing into demand models and rationalizes behavioral patterns that standard random-utility models have difficulty capturing.

<a class="paper-link" href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11129-025-09292-9">Published article →</a>

:::


::: {.paper}

### Recommend or Simplify? Digital Information Design with Cross-Category Spillovers

<div class="paper-meta">
with Dominik Naeher<br>
Working paper
</div>

We study how a multi-category seller should design information tools when consumers face limits in processing product information. Because information provision in one category changes attention and pricing incentives in others, category-specific interventions can generate cross-category spillovers and lead simplification and recommendation tools to have markedly different effects on firm profits and consumer welfare.

:::
